Deploying and Configuring Transit Gateway

An orientation to the steps, why each one matters, and how this fits into a hub-and-spoke architecture.

In this lesson you'll learn how to create a Transit Gateway, choose an Amazon Side ASN for BGP, attach VPCs with ENIs in multiple AZs, propagate routes into the TGW route table, and then update VPC route tables so traffic flows correctly. We'll also demonstrate sharing the TGW with other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager.

screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll connect each objective to practical verification steps and common pitfalls to check for. When creating the Transit Gateway, verify the Amazon side ASN and note whether DNS support and VPN ECMP are enabled; these options change how name resolution and VPN traffic behave. Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Learning Objectives

Objectives: Verification & Pitfalls

Each objective paired with how to confirm success and a common pitfall to avoid.

Create TGW — Verify
  • Confirm TransitGatewayId and AmazonSideAsn in the console.
  • Check DNS Support or VPN ECMP flags in the TGW options.
Pitfall: Choosing an ASN that conflicts with on-prem networks.
Attach VPCs — Verify
  • Confirm ENIs in at least two subnets across AZs.
  • Ensure subnets are not private-only if you need reachability during testing.
Pitfall: Selecting only one AZ and reducing availability.
Routing — Verify
  • Check TGW route table propagation for attached CIDRs.
  • Add VPC route entries for remote CIDRs pointing to the Transit Gateway ID.
Pitfall: Assuming propagation alone enables VPC-to-VPC traffic.
RAM — Verify
  • Confirm the Resource Share includes the TGW and recipient account IDs or OUs.
  • Ensure recipients accept the share before creating attachments.
Pitfall: Forgetting to accept the share in the recipient account.
Practical Mnemonic

ASN → Attach → Propagate → Route → Verify

screens.title: Create a Transit Gateway from the Console
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a Transit Gateway starts in the VPC console under the Transit Gateways section. The two fields that most affect later integration are the Amazon side ASN and the options for DNS support and VPN ECMP. The Amazon side ASN is the Autonomous System Number the TGW advertises when you set up BGP with on-premises routers; using a private ASN range is common for internal AWS deployments and avoids conflicts with public ASNs. DNS support enables name resolution across attached VPCs when combined with Route 53 resolver endpoints and helps with service discovery in multi-VPC deployments. VPN ECMP allows multiple VPN tunnels to operate in active/active mode, increasing throughput. For many initial setups, leaving default settings such as automatic acceptance of shared attachments and default route table association/propagation is fine, but you should understand them: association controls which TGW route table attachment routes are evaluated against, and propagation controls which attachment CIDRs are learned automatically. A mistake to watch for is entering an ASN that collides with on-prem networks. After creating the TGW, note the TransitGatewayId for subsequent attachment and routing steps. Do you have the right ASN and options to match your hybrid plan?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Create a Transit Gateway
Definition

Transit Gateway creation options

Each option affects routing behavior or integration with hybrid networks.

Amazon Side ASN — used for BGP when pairing TGW to on-prem routers. Prefer private ASNs for internal setups.
DNS Support — enables cross-VPC name resolution when configured with resolvers.
VPN ECMP — allows multiple equal-cost VPN tunnels for active/active VPN paths.
Common misconception
Some expect TGW creation alone to enable all cross-account attachments. Resource sharing and acceptance are still required for attachments from other accounts.
Console walkthrough (visualized)
1. Open VPC Console → Transit Gateways
2. Click Create transit gateway
3. Set Name, Description
4. Set Amazon side ASN (e.g., 64512)
5. Enable DNS support? (enable/disable)
6. Enable VPN ECMP? (enable/disable)
7. Leave Auto accept shared attachments=enable for now
8. Create and note TransitGatewayId
Example
Use ASN 64512 for an internal TGW that will peer with no on-prem BGP initially.
Key Takeaway
Pick an ASN and TGW flags that match your hybrid plan; note them for later BGP and routing configuration.

screens.title: Attaching VPCs and Selecting Subnets
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching a VPC to a Transit Gateway creates managed ENIs in the subnets you select. When creating a Transit Gateway attachment, choose the Transit Gateway, set the attachment type to VPC, then pick the VPC and at least one subnet in each Availability Zone where you want connectivity. AWS recommends selecting at least two subnets in different AZs to ensure high availability. The TGW will place an ENI in each selected subnet which becomes the ingress and egress point for traffic between the TGW and your VPC. Those ENIs appear as normal Elastic Network Interfaces in the subnet but are managed by AWS. A common operational error is to select only a single subnet or subnets in a single AZ; this can create asymmetric routing or single-AZ failures. Also ensure the subnets chosen allow the necessary traffic and that security groups and NACLs permit test traffic like ICMP during verification. After attachment, note the attachment ID to verify route propagation into the TGW route table. Attaching VPCs and Selecting Subnets means select subnets across azs for each vpc attachment so the tgw creates enis in multiple azs, providing availability and correct traffic flow.. In practical terms, how tgw enis are created and why az selection matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition

VPC Attachment and TGW ENIs

Choose subnets in multiple AZs; AWS will create ENIs there to carry traffic.

Why two subnets minimum?
High availability and avoidance of single-AZ failure modes for TGW traffic ingress/egress.
What the ENI does

Attachment Visual
VPC-App1

screens.title: Transit Gateway and Route Tables
screens.narratorSegment: Transit Gateway routing is controlled by TGW route tables which determine where traffic from attachments is forwarded. When you create a TGW it includes a default route table. Attachments can be associated with a specific route table and can also have their CIDRs propagated into that route table. Propagation causes the TGW to learn an attachment's CIDR and add a route that points to the attachment. However, association chooses which route table's rules an attachment uses for outbound routing. Many deployments use the default route table for simplicity, but larger networks often use multiple TGW route tables to implement segmentation or isolation between spokes. Importantly, propagation into the TGW does not change the route tables inside individual VPCs; you must add VPC route entries that point to the Transit Gateway ID for traffic to leave a VPC towards another. In multi-AZ scenarios the TGW route for the CIDR will resolve to the attachment, and the TGW will forward traffic to the appropriate ENI in the spoke VPC. A frequent misconception is to assume TGW propagation alone enables egress from a VPC; always update the VPC route tables as well.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › TGW Route Tables
Core Concept

Association vs Propagation

Association selects which TGW route table an attachment uses. Propagation causes the TGW to learn the attachment CIDRs.

TGW Route Table Example
When VPC-App1 and VPC-App2 are associated and propagated to the default TGW route table, the TGW contains routes for their CIDRs that point to each attachment.
Misconception
Propagation into TGW does not automatically change VPC route tables; you must add VPC routes pointing to the Transit Gateway ID.
Visual: Route flow
TGW Default Route Table
10.1.0.0/16 → VPC-App1-Attachment
10.2.0.0/16 → VPC-App2-Attachment
VPC Route Table Example
VPC-App1 Route Table
Destination     Target
10.1.0.0/16     Local
10.2.0.0/16     tgw-0123456789abcdef0
Key Takeaway

Use association to place attachments in the right TGW table and propagation to learn CIDRs; update VPC routes to send traffic to the TGW.

screens.title: VPC Route Table vs TGW Route Table
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between the VPC route table and the Transit Gateway route table is critical for correct inter-VPC routing. The TGW route table contains routes to attachments — it learns attachment CIDRs via propagation and decides where traffic received by the TGW should be forwarded. By contrast, a VPC route table decides how traffic originating in that VPC leaves the VPC. For two VPCs to communicate through a TGW, the TGW must know the destination attachment via propagation and each VPC must have explicit routes sending remote CIDRs to the TGW ID. For example, VPC-App1 needs a route for 10.2.0.0/16 with the target set to the Transit Gateway ID; otherwise, packets destined for VPC-App2 will not leave VPC-App1 even if the TGW already has a propagated route. A frequent misconception is expecting TGW propagation alone to permit traffic. In practice, both route tables must be aligned: TGW route table learns and forwards, and VPC route tables direct traffic into the TGW. Confirm routes in both places when debugging connectivity. VPC Route Table vs TGW Route Table means the tgw route table forwards between attachments; vpc route tables must explicitly send remote prefixes to the tgw for connectivity to work.. In practical terms, why both are required for inter-vpc connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › VPC vs TGW Route Tables
TGW Route Table

Forwards between attachments

Uses propagated attachment CIDRs to route traffic to the correct attachment ID.

  • Propagation learns CIDRs from attachments.
  • Association determines which table an attachment uses.
VPC Route Table

Directs traffic out of a VPC

Must have routes that target the Transit Gateway ID for remote CIDRs before traffic will be forwarded by the TGW.

  • Local routes stay inside the VPC.
  • Non-local routes must point to the TGW to reach other VPCs.
Concrete Example
VPC-App1 Route Table
Destination     Target
10.1.0.0/16     Local
10.2.0.0/16     tgw-0123456789abcdef0

TGW Default Route Table
10.1.0.0/16     VPC-App1-Attachment
10.2.0.0/16     VPC-App2-Attachment
Key Takeaway

Both the TGW route table and VPC route tables must be configured: TGW forwards, VPC sends traffic to the TGW.

keyIdea.text: A repeatable CLI sequence creates a TGW, VPCs, attachments, and routes; verification requires launching instances and testing connectivity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › CLI Hands-on
Create Transit Gateway (example)
# Replace with your desired region
AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
TGW_NAME="MyAdvancedNetworkingTGW"

aws ec2 create-transit-gateway \
    --description "$TGW_NAME" \
    --options "DnsSupport=enable,VpnEcmpSupport=enable,DefaultRouteTableAssociation=enable,DefaultRouteTablePropagation=enable,AmazonSideAsn=64512" \
    --tag-specifications "ResourceType=transit-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=$TGW_NAME}]" \
    --region $AWS_REGION
Create VPCs, subnets, attachments, and routes (example snippets)
# Create VPCs, subnets (one per AZ shown abbreviated)
VPC_A_CIDR="10.1.0.0/16"; VPC_B_CIDR="10.2.0.0/16"

# Attach VPC A
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --vpc-id $VPC_A_ID \
  --subnet-ids $SUBNET_A_ID1 $SUBNET_A_ID2 \
  --tag-specifications "ResourceType=transit-gateway-attachment,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=${VPC_A_NAME}-TGW-Attachment}]"

# Update VPC route tables to point to TGW
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $VPC_A_RT_ID --destination-cidr-block $VPC_B_CIDR --transit-gateway-id tgw-0123456789abcdef0
Verification & Common mistake
After creating attachments, check the TGW route table for propagated CIDRs and ensure each VPC route table has routes pointing to the TGW. A common mistake is to skip adding VPC routes and expect the TGW propagation alone to allow communication.
Key Takeaway

Use the CLI sequence as a lab script and verify with instance-level connectivity tests.

screens.title: Amazon Side ASN and BGP Integration
screens.narratorSegment: The Amazon side ASN is the Autonomous System Number that the Transit Gateway uses when participating in BGP sessions with on-premises routers or Direct Connect gateways. Choosing an ASN is particularly important when you plan to peer the TGW with on-prem via VPN or Direct Connect because ASNs must not conflict in BGP peering relationships. You may choose a private ASN, typically in the 64512–65534 range, for internal AWS routing. Using a private ASN isolates your TGW ASN space from public ASNs and is usually the simplest safe choice. If you already have an existing ASN on-premise, ensure the TGW ASN does not conflict. screens.title: Using AWS RAM to Share a Transit Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: In multi-account organizations it's common to centralize network resources in a dedicated networking account. AWS Resource Access Manager lets that account share the Transit Gateway so application accounts can attach their VPCs. The networking team creates a Resource Share in the R A M console or via CLI and includes the Transit Gateway as the shared resource. They then add the recipient AWS account IDs or Organization OUs as principals. The recipients must accept the share in their accounts; only after acceptance can they create a Transit Gateway attachment from their VPC to the shared TGW. This workflow preserves centralized control—attachments are still initiated by the application account but the TGW remains owned and managed centrally. A common operational oversight is forgetting to accept the share, then wondering why attachments cannot be created. Always confirm the share is accepted and that the shared TGW is visible in the recipient account before creating attachments. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting TGW connectivity starts with a checklist. First, confirm that each VPC route table contains routes for the peer VPC’s CIDR with the target set to the Transit Gateway ID. Next, verify the TGW route table has learned the attachment CIDRs through propagation and that each attachment is associated with the correct TGW route table. Check that TGW ENIs exist in the expected subnets and AZs. Security groups and NACLs are often overlooked; ensure they permit the test traffic such as ICMP or TCP on the application ports you plan to use. If you used AWS R A M to share the TGW, verify the resource share is accepted. Another typical error is not selecting subnets across AZs, causing asymmetric routing during failures. For hybrid BGP connections, ensure the Amazon side ASN does not conflict with on-prem ASNs. A practical verification step is to launch EC2 instances in each VPC, open the necessary security group ports, and ping or curl between instances while watching route tables and attachment state. This method pinpoints whether the issue is routing, security, or attachment configuration.

screens.title: Lab Activity: Verify Inter-VPC Communication
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walks you through verifying inter-VPC connectivity after you've created the TGW and attachments. Begin by launching a small EC2 instance in each VPC's test subnet and ensure security groups permit ICMP or the application port you want to test. Note the instance private IPs. On the source instance, attempt a ping or a TCP connect to the destination instance. If the ping fails, inspect the source VPC's route table to ensure it has a route for the destination CIDR pointing to the Transit Gateway ID. Next, check the TGW route table to confirm the destination CIDR is propagated and points to the correct attachment. If the TGW route exists but packets don't arrive, examine the ENIs in the destination VPC subnets and the destination instance security group to ensure inbound traffic is permitted. This step-by-step verification isolates whether the problem is a VPC route, a TGW propagation/association issue, or a security control blocking traffic. Finally, correct the identified configuration and run the test again until traffic flows successfully. screens.title: Operational Best Practices and Cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: When operating Transit Gateways at scale follow a few practical best practices. First, document the Amazon side ASN, TGW ID, route table associations, and attachment IDs so teams can reference them for BGP and routing changes. Keep security groups and NACLs simple and explicit for inter-VPC traffic so debugging is straightforward. Finally, clean up lab resources after a demo: delete TGW attachments, VPCs, and the TGW itself to avoid prolonged costs. A helpful habit is a teardown script that reverses your creation steps. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll take a practical, step-by-step approach to deploying an AWS Transit Gateway and connecting VPCs so that they can communicate securely. You will learn which options matter during creation, how Transit Gateway ENIs appear in your subnets, and why updating VPC route tables is essential for traffic to flow. We will also cover cross-account sharing with AWS Resource Access Manager, a common enterprise pattern for central network control. As we go, I will point out common mistakes such as selecting too few subnets or forgetting VPC routes, and show how to verify connectivity with a simple EC2 ping test. By the end you will understand the core pieces: the Amazon side ASN for BGP, DNS support for cross-VPC resolution, Equal-Cost Multi-Path for VPNs, and how propagation into the TGW route table differs from VPC route table configuration. Keep in mind that Transit Gateway handles routing, but security groups and NACLs still enforce what traffic is allowed. Ready to build a resilient hub-and-spoke network? Let’s begin.

These learning objectives describe the practical skills you will develop while deploying and configuring a Transit Gateway. First, you'll perform the step-by-step creation of a Transit Gateway from the VPC console and understand each option you choose, such as the Amazon side ASN and DNS or VPN ECMP settings. Second, you'll attach VPCs and their subnets to the TGW and learn why selecting subnets across Availability Zones matters for ENI placement and availability. Third, you'll configure routing both on the Transit Gateway route table and in each VPC's route tables, ensuring that propagated TGW routes are complemented by explicit VPC routes that send traffic to the TGW. Finally, you'll learn how AWS Resource Access Manager is used to share a centrally owned Transit Gateway with other accounts so teams can attach their VPCs centrally. Each objective includes hands-on practice and a verification step so you can confirm connectivity and avoid common mistakes like missing VPC routes or insufficient subnet selection.

Now we'll connect each objective to practical verification steps and common pitfalls to check for. When creating the Transit Gateway, verify the Amazon side ASN and note whether DNS support and VPN ECMP are enabled; these options change how name resolution and VPN traffic behave. When attaching VPCs, check that you selected subnets in multiple Availability Zones so the TGW creates ENIs across AZs for resiliency; if you pick only one AZ, an AZ failure can cut off traffic. For routing, remember that TGW propagation populates the TGW route table, but it does not automatically change routes inside each VPC. To verify connectivity, add a route in the VPC route table that points the other VPC CIDR to the Transit Gateway ID, then launch simple instances and test connectivity. For cross-account sharing, validate that the R A M resource share is accepted and that the receiving account can create attachments. Each verification step avoids a common mistake and ensures the network behaves as intended.

Creating a Transit Gateway starts in the VPC console under the Transit Gateways section. The two fields that most affect later integration are the Amazon side ASN and the options for DNS support and VPN ECMP. The Amazon side ASN is the Autonomous System Number the TGW advertises when you set up BGP with on-premises routers; using a private ASN range is common for internal AWS deployments and avoids conflicts with public ASNs. DNS support enables name resolution across attached VPCs when combined with Route 53 resolver endpoints and helps with service discovery in multi-VPC deployments. VPN ECMP allows multiple VPN tunnels to operate in active/active mode, increasing throughput. For many initial setups, leaving default settings such as automatic acceptance of shared attachments and default route table association/propagation is fine, but you should understand them: association controls which TGW route table attachment routes are evaluated against, and propagation controls which attachment CIDRs are learned automatically. A mistake to watch for is entering an ASN that collides with on-prem networks. After creating the TGW, note the TransitGatewayId for subsequent attachment and routing steps. Do you have the right ASN and options to match your hybrid plan?

Attaching a VPC to a Transit Gateway creates managed ENIs in the subnets you select. When creating a Transit Gateway attachment, choose the Transit Gateway, set the attachment type to VPC, then pick the VPC and at least one subnet in each Availability Zone where you want connectivity. AWS recommends selecting at least two subnets in different AZs to ensure high availability. The TGW will place an ENI in each selected subnet which becomes the ingress and egress point for traffic between the TGW and your VPC. Those ENIs appear as normal Elastic Network Interfaces in the subnet but are managed by AWS. A common operational error is to select only a single subnet or subnets in a single AZ; this can create asymmetric routing or single-AZ failures. Also ensure the subnets chosen allow the necessary traffic and that security groups and NACLs permit test traffic like ICMP during verification. After attachment, note the attachment ID to verify route propagation into the TGW route table. Attaching VPCs and Selecting Subnets means select subnets across azs for each vpc attachment so the tgw creates enis in multiple azs, providing availability and correct traffic flow.. In practical terms, how tgw enis are created and why az selection matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transit Gateway routing is controlled by TGW route tables which determine where traffic from attachments is forwarded. When you create a TGW it includes a default route table. Attachments can be associated with a specific route table and can also have their CIDRs propagated into that route table. Propagation causes the TGW to learn an attachment's CIDR and add a route that points to the attachment. However, association chooses which route table's rules an attachment uses for outbound routing. Many deployments use the default route table for simplicity, but larger networks often use multiple TGW route tables to implement segmentation or isolation between spokes. Importantly, propagation into the TGW does not change the route tables inside individual VPCs; you must add VPC route entries that point to the Transit Gateway ID for traffic to leave a VPC towards another. In multi-AZ scenarios the TGW route for the CIDR will resolve to the attachment, and the TGW will forward traffic to the appropriate ENI in the spoke VPC. A frequent misconception is to assume TGW propagation alone enables egress from a VPC; always update the VPC route tables as well.

Understanding the difference between the VPC route table and the Transit Gateway route table is critical for correct inter-VPC routing. The TGW route table contains routes to attachments — it learns attachment CIDRs via propagation and decides where traffic received by the TGW should be forwarded. By contrast, a VPC route table decides how traffic originating in that VPC leaves the VPC. For two VPCs to communicate through a TGW, the TGW must know the destination attachment via propagation and each VPC must have explicit routes sending remote CIDRs to the TGW ID. For example, VPC-App1 needs a route for 10.2.0.0/16 with the target set to the Transit Gateway ID; otherwise, packets destined for VPC-App2 will not leave VPC-App1 even if the TGW already has a propagated route. A frequent misconception is expecting TGW propagation alone to permit traffic. In practice, both route tables must be aligned: TGW route table learns and forwards, and VPC route tables direct traffic into the TGW. Confirm routes in both places when debugging connectivity. VPC Route Table vs TGW Route Table means the tgw route table forwards between attachments; vpc route tables must explicitly send remote prefixes to the tgw for connectivity to work.. In practical terms, why both are required for inter-vpc connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on sequence demonstrates the essential CLI commands you would run to create a Transit Gateway, two VPCs, attach them, and add routes. The first command creates the TGW with options for DNS and VPN ECMP and a chosen Amazon side ASN. Next you create VPCs and subnets in two Availability Zones for high availability. Then create transit gateway VPC attachments using at least two subnet IDs per VPC. Finally, update each VPC main route table to add a route for the peer VPC's CIDR that targets the Transit Gateway ID. After running these commands, you should verify the TransitGatewayId and the attachment IDs. Launching a pair of EC2 instances and pinging between them validates routing and security group configuration. A common mistake in labs is assuming the TGW propagation removes the need to add VPC routes — it does not. The Amazon side ASN is the Autonomous System Number that the Transit Gateway uses when participating in BGP sessions with on-premises routers or Direct Connect gateways. Choosing an ASN is particularly important when you plan to peer the TGW with on-prem via VPN or Direct Connect because ASNs must not conflict in BGP peering relationships. You may choose a private ASN, typically in the 64512–65534 range, for internal AWS routing. Using a private ASN isolates your TGW ASN space from public ASNs and is usually the simplest safe choice. If you already have an existing ASN on-premise, ensure the TGW ASN does not conflict. In practice, pick a private ASN for initial deployments and document it so that later BGP configurations can reference the correct number. A misconception is that an ASN only matters for advanced users; in reality it affects route advertisement and path selection when connecting hybrid networks. A concrete example: pick ASN 64512 for a staging TGW and record that value before creating any VPN or Direct Connect BGP sessions. In multi-account organizations it's common to centralize network resources in a dedicated networking account. AWS Resource Access Manager lets that account share the Transit Gateway so application accounts can attach their VPCs. The networking team creates a Resource Share in the R A M console or via CLI and includes the Transit Gateway as the shared resource. They then add the recipient AWS account IDs or Organization OUs as principals. The recipients must accept the share in their accounts; only after acceptance can they create a Transit Gateway attachment from their VPC to the shared TGW. This workflow preserves centralized control—attachments are still initiated by the application account but the TGW remains owned and managed centrally. A common operational oversight is forgetting to accept the share, then wondering why attachments cannot be created. Always confirm the share is accepted and that the shared TGW is visible in the recipient account before creating attachments. Troubleshooting TGW connectivity starts with a checklist. First, confirm that each VPC route table contains routes for the peer VPC’s CIDR with the target set to the Transit Gateway ID. Next, verify the TGW route table has learned the attachment CIDRs through propagation and that each attachment is associated with the correct TGW route table. Check that TGW ENIs exist in the expected subnets and AZs. Security groups and NACLs are often overlooked; ensure they permit the test traffic such as ICMP or TCP on the application ports you plan to use. If you used AWS R A M to share the TGW, verify the resource share is accepted. Another typical error is not selecting subnets across AZs, causing asymmetric routing during failures. For hybrid BGP connections, ensure the Amazon side ASN does not conflict with on-prem ASNs. A practical verification step is to launch EC2 instances in each VPC, open the necessary security group ports, and ping or curl between instances while watching route tables and attachment state. This method pinpoints whether the issue is routing, security, or attachment configuration.

This lab walks you through verifying inter-VPC connectivity after you've created the TGW and attachments. Begin by launching a small EC2 instance in each VPC's test subnet and ensure security groups permit ICMP or the application port you want to test. Note the instance private IPs. On the source instance, attempt a ping or a TCP connect to the destination instance. If the ping fails, inspect the source VPC's route table to ensure it has a route for the destination CIDR pointing to the Transit Gateway ID. Next, check the TGW route table to confirm the destination CIDR is propagated and points to the correct attachment. If the TGW route exists but packets don't arrive, examine the ENIs in the destination VPC subnets and the destination instance security group to ensure inbound traffic is permitted. This step-by-step verification isolates whether the problem is a VPC route, a TGW propagation/association issue, or a security control blocking traffic. Finally, correct the identified configuration and run the test again until traffic flows successfully. When operating Transit Gateways at scale follow a few practical best practices. First, document the Amazon side ASN, TGW ID, route table associations, and attachment IDs so teams can reference them for BGP and routing changes. Use multiple TGW route tables where you need segmentation between groups of spokes or to implement routing policies. Select two or more subnets across AZs for each attachment to maintain availability. Monitor TGW and attachment status in the console and use CloudWatch metrics for traffic trends. Keep security groups and NACLs simple and explicit for inter-VPC traffic so debugging is straightforward. Finally, clean up lab resources after a demo: delete TGW attachments, VPCs, and the TGW itself to avoid prolonged costs. A helpful habit is a teardown script that reverses your creation steps. Let's summarize three compact concepts you should remember. First, the Amazon side ASN is the TGW’s ASN used for BGP with on-prem; choose a private ASN when possible and document it. Second, Transit Gateway attachments create TGW ENIs in the subnets you select; choose at least two subnets across different Availability Zones for high availability. Third, routing requires both TGW route table propagation and explicit VPC route table entries targeting the Transit Gateway ID; propagation alone is not sufficient. Keep these three ideas in mind during creation, attachment, and verification. They are the rules that explain most connectivity issues you will encounter and will help you design predictable, maintainable hub-and-spoke networks. Second, choose subnets across at least two Availability Zones so the Transit Gateway creates ENIs that provide high availability for traffic into each VPC. Third, after attachments are created, add routes inside each VPC that point remote CIDRs to the Transit Gateway ID — propagation alone is insufficient.
